topic.subject: social
topic.title: Inside our Earth and changing landforms
topic.scope: crust, mantle, core, rocks and rock cycle, earthquakes, volcanoes, work of rivers, wind, glaciers, sea waves

misconceptions.statement: The Earth's core is a giant ball of liquid fire.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the high temperature with the state of fire.
misconceptions.fix: The core is made of dense metals like nickel and iron under extreme pressure, not fire.

probe.question: What is the primary source of heat in the Earth's core?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Rocks are permanent and never change.
misconceptions.why: The human lifespan is too short to observe geological time scales.
misconceptions.fix: Rocks are constantly changing through the rock cycle over millions of years.

probe.question: Can a sedimentary rock become an igneous rock?
probe.wrong_answer: No, rocks stay the same forever

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Earthquakes are caused by underground explosions or giant caverns collapsing.
misconceptions.why: Students try to explain large events using familiar small-scale phenomena.
misconceptions.fix: Earthquakes are caused by the sudden release of energy from moving tectonic plates.

probe.question: What causes the ground to shake during an earthquake?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Rivers only erode the land; they do not build it up.
misconceptions.why: Erosion is more visually dramatic than deposition.
misconceptions.fix: Rivers erode land in upper courses and deposit sediment in lower courses to form plains.

probe.question: What happens to the sediment carried by a river?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: The Earth's crust is the thickest layer of the Earth.
misconceptions.why: Students live on the crust and it feels huge, and diagrams are often not drawn to scale, so it looks substantial.
misconceptions.fix: The crust is the thinnest layer, only about 35 km thick on continents and 5 km under oceans. The mantle (about 2900 km) is the thickest layer.

probe.question: Which layer of the Earth is the thickest?
probe.wrong_answer: The crust, because it is the layer we live on and can see.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible or familiar layer must be the biggest
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom diagnostic questions on Earth structure

misconceptions.statement: People have reached the centre of the Earth by drilling, so we know its layers by direct observation.
misconceptions.why: Students see deep mines and borehole news and assume scientists have gone all the way down.
misconceptions.fix: The deepest mines and boreholes reach only a few km to about 12 km. The interior is studied indirectly through seismic waves, meteorites and volcanic material.

probe.question: How do scientists know about the Earth's core?
probe.wrong_answer: They drilled down to the core and took samples.

misconceptions.root_belief: Scientific knowledge always comes from direct observation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's conceptions of Earth's interior

misconceptions.statement: All igneous rocks form on the surface from lava, so granite and basalt form the same way.
misconceptions.why: Students link igneous rocks only with visible volcanoes and lava flows.
misconceptions.fix: Extrusive igneous rocks like basalt cool quickly on the surface; intrusive rocks like granite cool slowly inside the Earth and have bigger crystals.

probe.question: How is granite formed?
probe.wrong_answer: From lava that flows out of a volcano and cools on the surface.

misconceptions.root_belief: Igneous rocks come only from surface lava
misconceptions.source_hint: geoscience education studies on rock formation

misconceptions.statement: Metamorphic rocks form when rocks melt and then harden again.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up metamorphic with igneous because both involve heat.
misconceptions.fix: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure without melting, e.g. limestone to marble, shale to slate. Melting and cooling forms igneous rock.

probe.question: How does limestone become marble?
probe.wrong_answer: Limestone melts completely into liquid and then cools to become marble.

misconceptions.statement: In the rock cycle, rocks must change in a fixed order: igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic.
misconceptions.why: Textbook rock cycle diagrams are read as a one-way circular sequence.
misconceptions.fix: Any rock can change into any other type through many pathways; for example, igneous rock can become metamorphic directly, and sedimentary rock can melt to form igneous rock.

probe.question: Can a metamorphic rock be turned directly into an igneous rock?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must first become sedimentary rock.

misconceptions.root_belief: Natural cycles follow one fixed sequence
misconceptions.source_hint: geoscience education research on the rock cycle

misconceptions.statement: Volcanoes and earthquakes happen randomly all over the world.
misconceptions.why: News reports mention them in scattered places and students do not connect them to plate boundaries.
misconceptions.fix: They occur mostly along plate boundaries, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire, where moving plates interact.

probe.question: Why are many volcanoes found around the Pacific Ocean?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just chance; volcanoes can erupt anywhere equally.

misconceptions.root_belief: Natural hazards have no spatial pattern

misconceptions.statement: Glaciers are frozen and stationary blocks of ice that do not move.
misconceptions.why: Ice looks solid and rigid, and students think only liquid water flows.
misconceptions.fix: Glaciers are slow-moving rivers of ice that flow downhill under their own weight, carving valleys and carrying rock debris, forming moraines and U-shaped valleys.

probe.question: How can a glacier shape a valley?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot, because ice stays still and does not move.

misconceptions.root_belief: Solid things cannot flow or move
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about glaciers

misconceptions.statement: Wind erosion and deposition happen only in hot deserts, never elsewhere.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks illustrate sand dunes and mushroom rocks with deserts, so students tie wind work only to deserts.
misconceptions.fix: Wind erodes and deposits wherever loose, dry sediment and little vegetation exist, including coasts, dry river beds and farmland; loess is wind-blown deposit far from deserts.

probe.question: Can wind create landforms on a sea coast?
probe.wrong_answer: No, wind landforms form only in hot deserts.

misconceptions.root_belief: Landform processes are limited to textbook example settings
